businessType: Mid-cap aerospace & defense contractor and tier-1 supplier to U.S. and allied government programs and prime contractors. Public company. Primary products: precision structural assemblies, propulsion components, and mission subsystems sold under multi-year government and prime-contractor programs. Revenue model: ~70% firm-fixed-price (FFP) multi-year contracts, ~30% cost-plus or contracts with escalation clauses. Approximately 6,500 employees.
stage: FY2025: Revenue $2,100M (up from $2,040M FY2024, +2.9% YoY on program ramp). EBITDA $168M, EBITDA margin 8.0% (down from $204M / 10.0% in FY2024, a 200 bps decline). Contract mix: ~70% revenue ($1,470M) firm-fixed-price multi-year without economic price adjustment (EPA) clauses; ~30% ($630M) cost-plus or escalating. Materials cost FY2025 $735M (35% of revenue), up +12% YoY like-for-like. Direct labor FY2025 $546M (26% of revenue), up +8% YoY. Backlog $5.6B (2.7x revenue). Book-to-bill 1.1.
ownerGoal: Restore EBITDA margin toward 10% and protect program profitability across the remaining multi-year backlog, while setting disciplined pricing for the next bid cycle. CEO must decide within ~120 days whether to file Requests for Equitable Adjustment (REAs) and how to price upcoming FFP bids before the re-pricing window closes.
ownerConstraints: Contractual constraint: Firm-fixed-price multi-year contracts cannot be reopened unilaterally. Price relief requires negotiated change orders, REAs, or contractually grounded claims; unilateral price increases would constitute breach.

Regulatory constraint: Subject to DFARS, FAR, and U.S. government contracting compliance, including TINA/certified cost-or-pricing data rules and CAS. Any pricing adjustment or claim must be fully compliant and documented.

Strategic constraint: Cannot walk away from strategic programs. Several FFP contracts are tied to flagship platforms central to customer relationships and future award eligibility; abandonment would forfeit positioning and incur termination liability.

Competitive constraint: High recompete risk. An aggressive pricing posture or perceived non-performance jeopardizes follow-on awards and re-compete outcomes on multi-billion-dollar program franchises.

Quality/safety constraint: Defense and flight-critical work is governed by AS9100, customer source inspection, and airworthiness requirements. Labor and material reductions cannot compromise quality, safety, or first-article conformance.
Capital/financial constraint: Investment-grade balance sheet must be preserved; major restructuring or write-downs would signal program distress to customers and investors.
immediateConcern: EBITDA margin fell 200 bps (10.0% to 8.0%) in a single year despite revenue growth and a strong $5.6B backlog. Materials are up 12% and labor up 8%, but roughly 70% of revenue sits in firm-fixed-price multi-year contracts priced before the inflation surge and lacking economic price adjustment (EPA) clauses, so cost increases cannot be passed through. Demand is healthy (book-to-bill 1.1), so the compression is not a demand or volume problem. The CEO must decide next-cycle bid pricing and whether to pursue REAs within ~120 days before the re-pricing window closes and before bidding additional FFP work that could lock in more underpriced backlog.
